claims.text: In equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, phase stability is governed by atomic-size-mismatch-induced lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion governs retention of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness in this alloy system.
Atomic size mismatch produces local lattice distortions and strain fields.
Local lattice distortions create a rugged atomic-scale energy landscape.
The rugged energy landscape reduces differences between vacancy and interstitial mobilities.
More similar vacancy and interstitial mobilities enhance point-defect recombination.
Enhanced point-defect recombination suppresses the formation of dislocation loops.
Enhanced point-defect recombination suppresses nucleation of secondary phases.
Secondary phases and dislocation loops would degrade mechanical and environmental properties.
The baseline equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy has moderate inherent lattice distortion.
The baseline alloy may exhibit either a dual-phase structure such as FCC plus B2 or a single-phase structure.
Changing Al content or partially substituting an element can increase atomic size mismatch and lattice distortion while leaving the overall chemistry comparable.
Relative to the equiatomic baseline, an alloy with greater lattice distortion will have significantly lower irradiation-induced defect concentrations.
Relative to the baseline, an alloy with greater lattice distortion will exhibit less precipitation or phase segregation during irradiation and thermal cycling.
Relative to the baseline, an alloy with greater lattice distortion will retain its mechanical properties better during irradiation and thermal cycling.
A refractory W–Ta–V–Cr HEA showed no irradiation-created dislocation loops in TEM after irradiation to 8 dpa.
The proposed relationship is limited to near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni compositions whose adjustments do not independently induce entirely new phases.
The quantitative relationships among lattice distortion, point-defect mobility, and secondary-phase suppression may depend on irradiation and thermal regimes.
